groundTruthNarrative: The rise in ED length of stay for admitted patients at Halden Valley is almost entirely boarding time, not ED work. ED nursing hours per visit, vacancies and grid compliance are unchanged, as are volume, acuity and inpatient bed capacity. On 2 March 2026 the hospitalist group moved rounding to 09:30 and saw new admissions first, which pushed discharge orders on the medical wards from late morning to mid-afternoon; surgical wards were unaffected. Beds now free up after 15:00, so admitted ED patients wait in ED rooms through the afternoon, which overloads ED nurses and fills rooms, producing the overload the CNO and ED director describe. A 4 West huddle that restores discharge-first sequencing, scheduled by a pre-set rotation, halved boarding for that ward with no change elsewhere. The front-end decline is confounded by the May removal of the triage provider, and the September EVS cut's contribution is unmeasured. Travel nurses funded by cutting case managers, or pausing the huddle, would treat the symptom and weaken the effective fix.

answers.rationale: ED RN productive hours per visit are flat (2.61 to 2.64), vacancies fell and grid compliance is 96-97% (E4, payroll-based), while ED work-up time for admitted patients rose only 2.7 to 2.9 h and non-admitted LOS 2.9 to 3.1 h (E3, E5); about 3.0 of the 3.2 h rise is boarding, an interval timed by bed management after the admit decision (E5). The nurses' overload (E12, E13) is real but is caused by holding admitted patients, not by fewer nursing hours. The evidence counts against the claim.

Boarding accounts for ~3.0 of 3.2 h (E5). Boarding jumped in March, the month the rounding change took effect (E9, E6); medical-ward discharge orders moved from 11:50 to 15:25 while surgical wards, not covered by the memo, were unchanged (E8); the hospitalist director confirms the mechanism (E7); and medical-ward boarders account for 81% of boarding hours (E9). The pilot shows earlier discharges cut boarding (E10, E11). This explanation fits better than every rival.

Visits per month rose under 1% (5,210 to 5,260), the admission rate is 27% in both quarters and ESI 1-2 share moved 31% to 32% (E3); ED work-up time barely changed (E5). The evidence counts against a volume or acuity explanation.

Staffed beds are 388 in both periods, midnight occupancy 87% vs 88% and inpatient average stay 4.8 vs 4.8 days (E9). Boarding is concentrated 14:00-20:00 (E9) because beds free up late in the day (E8), a timing problem rather than less capacity.

Evening cleaning staff were cut on 1 September (E15), but there are no turnaround data after June (E15) and only one month of boarding data since (Sep 4.6 h vs 4.3-4.4 h in Jun-Aug, E9), a difference within normal monthly variation and also overlapping the 4 West pilot. Boarding had already risen by March, so the cut cannot be the main cause, but whether it adds materially now cannot be determined; the claim is live but unestablished.

Staffing hours per visit stayed flat (2.61 to 2.64) while the headline measure rose 4.1 to 7.3 h (E3, E4); the ED-controlled interval moved only 0.2 h (E5), and the charge nurse says the ED is at grid most days (E12). Covariation is absent, so the evidence counts against the link.

Temporal order (memo effective 2 March, E6; boarding jumps in March, E9), a stated mechanism (admissions first, discharges after lunch, E7), covariation on the medical wards (orders 11:50 to 15:25, E8), and a comparison group ruling out a hospital-wide trend: surgical wards outside the memo did not shift (E8). Restoring discharge-first sequencing on huddle days reversed the shift (E10). This meets the causal standard.

The pilot is a natural experiment: huddle days were set by a rotation fixed before the pilot (E11), ED arrivals, admissions and 4 West census were similar on huddle and non-huddle days (E11), and the trained hospitalists showed no difference before the pilot (E11), ruling out a physician effect. On huddle days, before-noon discharges rose 11% to 38% and boarding for 4 West fell 4.6 to 2.3 h, while boarding to the other medical wards on the same days was unchanged (E10, E11). This is an intervention result with controls.

Door-to-provider (22 to 34 min) and left-without-being-seen (1.6% to 3.4%) worsened in the same period as boarding rose (E14, E9), and staff describe rooms filled by boarders (E12), so the two co-occur. But the provider-in-triage shift was cut on 1 May (E14), inside the same window, and only quarterly data exist, so the two causes cannot be separated. Causation is not established.

It targets the demonstrated cause (late discharges, E8) with an intervention shown to cut boarding under controlled conditions (E10, E11), keeps the 08:00 meeting and so does not undo the hospitalist retention change (E7), and tracks results. Medical wards carry 81% of boarding hours (E9). Among the offered actions it is the best supported.

A discharge lounge is a reasonable, low-risk step, but order-to-departure time is only 1.6 h and unchanged (E8); the bottleneck is that orders are written at 15:25 rather than the time after the order. It helps at the margin without addressing the main driver, so it is acceptable, not preferred; it does not depend on an unconfirmed hypothesis and carries no evident harm.

Making EVS staffing the primary fix would only be justified if H5 were confirmed, but there are no turnaround data after June and only one ambiguous month of boarding data (E15, E9). Boarding rose six months before the cut (E9), so it cannot be the main cause. Committing to it as the primary fix now is premature; turnaround data (Q1) would resolve it. It is not harmful (restoring cleaning capacity does not worsen outcomes or disable a control) and not acceptable as worded, because the evidence does not support it as the primary fix.

It spends $1.46M on ED nurse hours that are not short (E4, E5) and funds that spend by deferring two medical-ward case managers, leaving coverage at one per 22 versus a target of 15 and stretching the 4 West case manager across two wards (E16). The case manager prepares the huddle's discharge list (E10), so the funding source weakens the one intervention shown to reduce boarding. Likely to worsen outcomes.

Pausing the huddle disables the only intervention shown to cut boarding (4.6 to 2.3 h for 4 West, E10, E11) to put one nurse into the ED, where nursing hours are not the constraint (E4) and rooms are occupied by boarders (E12). It would likely lengthen boarding and the headline measure.

The decomposition (E5), the timing shift with a surgical comparison (E8), and a controlled pilot (E10, E11) together justify committing to a substantive intervention (extending the huddle). The open questions (EVS contribution, front-end causes) do not bear on that commitment.
